speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. Can you describe the sensation of dizziness you are experiencing—does the room feel like it is spinning around you, or do you feel lightheaded and faint?

speaker: Patient
text: 70-year-old woman. The patient presents with sudden episodes of dizziness that are position dependent. She describes experiencing a false sensation of motion and occasional spinning, indicative of vertigo. She denies any recent illnesses, injuries, or significant changes in health status, apart from age-related hearing loss (presbycusis).

speaker: Doctor
text: Do these dizzy spells last for just a few seconds when you move your head, or do they persist for minutes to hours? I also need to know if you have experienced any ringing in your ears or new hearing loss in one ear.

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Episodes of dizziness and spinning sensation. I also have Position dependent vertigo, No recent illness, No hearing loss besides presbycusis. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Migraine and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text: I need to clarify a few details to distinguish this from vestibular migraine, as the previous diagnosis seems inconsistent with the lack of headache history. Do you experience nausea or vomiting during these episodes, and does changing your head position relative to gravity (like rolling over in bed) specifically trigger the spinning?

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: No significant past medical or surgical history. No history of Meniere's disease, vestibular neuritis, or labyrinthitis. Social history: Retired school teacher. Lives alone. Non-smoker, occasional wine. Enjoys light gardening.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given the position-dependent nature of your vertigo and the absence of hearing loss, I suspect Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV). I will now perform a physical examination to check for nystagmus. REQUEST TEST: Dix-Hallpike Maneuver

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Positive for right-sided horizontal nystagmus when moving from sitting to supine position, suggestive of BPPV

speaker: Doctor
text:
The positive Dix-Hallpike maneuver confirms Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV). I will now perform the Epley maneuver to reposition the displaced otoconia and alleviate your symptoms.

DIAGNOSIS READY: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV)
